feed.text:
Today and every day, we recognize and celebrate the cultures, histories, and contributions of Indigenous peoples.

Long before these islands were called the Virgin Islands, they were home to the Ciboney, Taíno, and Carib (Kalinago) peoples, who fished our waters, farmed our land, and built thriving communities across St. Croix, St. Thomas, and St. John. Their legacy lives on in our landscape: in the petroglyphs carved at Reef Bay on St. John, in the ceremonial grounds uncovered at Cinnamon Bay, and at Salt River Bay on St. Croix, where Carib warriors stood their ground in 1493 in one of the first recorded acts of Indigenous resistance to European arrival in the Americas.

On Indigenous Peoples' Day, we honor these first Virgin Islanders, whose history is part of our history, and the Indigenous communities whose traditions have endured across generations and continue to shape our territory and our country.

Today and every day, we recognize and celebrate the cultures, histories, and contributions of Indigenous peoples.

Long before these islands were called the Virgin Islands, they were home to the Ciboney, Taíno, and Carib (Kalinago) peoples, who fished our waters, farmed our land, and built thriving communities across St. Croix, St. Thomas, and St. John. Their legacy lives on in our landscape: in the petroglyphs carved at Reef Bay on St. John, in the ceremonial grounds uncovered at Cinnamon Bay, and at Salt River Bay on St. Croix, where Carib warriors stood their ground in 1493 in one of the first recorded acts of Indigenous resistance to European arrival in the Americas.

On Indigenous Peoples' Day, we honor these first Virgin Islanders, whose history is part of our history, and the Indigenous communities whose traditions have endured across generations and continue to shape our territory and our country.

My speech at a 10/7 vigil in the Bronx:

Three years ago, October 7th—the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust—cruelly coincided with Simchat Torah.  What should have been a day of joy became one of overwhelming grief, shock, and trauma. On that day, Jews throughout the world were robbed of the joy of Simchat Torah.

When I led a Bronx delegation to Israel for the first time since October 7th, I will never forget the experience of meeting the survivors of the Nova massacre and finding myself inspired by their resilience, by their insistence on defying despair itself, by the message: “We will dance again.” Those words remind us that the joy of Simchat Torah can never be surrendered to terror. It must be reclaimed.  

The most powerful antidote to antisemitism is to be joyfully Jewish.  Franklin Roosevelt once said, “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.”  Jewish identity is a beautiful gift.  It is not something to be hidden out of fear. It is something to be openly celebrated with joy. With pride. With passion. And with love.

The purpose of terrorism is to strike terror into the heart of a people. The Jewish people and their allies must never stop dancing, never stop singing, and never stop living. Because the moment we stop, terror has won.
And terror can never have the final word on the fate of either the Jewish people or the Jewish State.

So I have a simple call to action:
Never give up. Never give in.
Never stop singing. Never stop dancing.
Relentlessly rejoice in your Judaism.
Am Yisrael Chai.

As the Co-Chair of the Congressional Friends of Ireland Caucus, I welcome tonight's decision by Secretary of State Chris Bryant to ban the controversial Orange Order march in Drumcree. With this announcement, 28 years of precedent has been upheld. This march is an affront to the Garvaghy Road residents and those who have committed their lives to advancing peace and reconciliation on the island of Ireland. This has been a deeply divisive issue for years, and after three decades of hard-earned progress, allowing the march to proceed would have put that very progress in jeopardy.
